newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesians vote, violence flares in East Timor.
newsitem.headline: Indonesians vote, violence flares in East Timor.

text.p: Millions of Indonesians voted in general elections on Thursday as police reported 13 people killed in election-eve violence in the troubled territory of East Timor.

East Timor police chief Colonel Yusuf Muharam said by telephone from Dili that police had shot dead four rebels in a clash in the centre of the local capital on Wednesday night during an attempt to disrupt the elections.
He said rebels shot dead at least seven civilians in the town of Los Palos and two in Baucau in separate attacks on Wednesday as opponents of the government destroyed a number of polling booths.

The rebels are fighting Indonesian rule in East Timor after Jakarta invaded the territory in 1975 and incorporated it as its 27th province the following year. The move has never been recognised by the United Nations.
National police spokesman Brigadier-General Nur Faizi said on Thursday the situation throughout the country was calm.
"Voting is going well. People are going to the polling stations. The situation is peaceful and there have been no incidents throughout the country," he told Reuters.
The East Timor police chief said voting was proceeding normally in the territory.

President Suharto, who urged people on Wednesday night to exercise their democratic right and duty by voting, cast his ballot at a polling booth in a garden 250 metres (yards) from his central Jakarta residence.
The president, accompanied by several members of his family, smiled and waved as he slipped his ballot paper into the box and then left for a tour of other polling stations in north Jakarta.

The East Timor shootings followed the most violent election campaign in three decades, which ended last Friday with more than 120 deaths in a riot and shopping mall fire in the South Kalimantan capital of Banjarmasin.
Nearly 125 million people are eligible to vote in the archipelago of more than 17,500 islands stretching for 5,000 km (3,000 miles) along the equator.

The ruling Golkar is assured of victory, but political analysts said they were carefully watching the minority Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) in case it felt it had been cheated in the poll.

Golkar, the PPP and the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), badly split by a leadership battle, are the only three groups legally permitted to contest the poll for 425 elected seats in the House of Representatives.
The other 75 parliamentary seats are filled by the military which does not vote.

Most of the violence during the 27-day election campaign which ended last Friday arose from clashes between Golkar and PPP partisans and security forces, mainly on Java island, home to 60 percent of the country's 200 million people.

The government imposed a five-day cooling off period ahead of Thursday's polls. Jakarta had been nervous with a spate of bomb threats and rumours, including a hoax bomb call on Wednesday that forced the temporary evacuation of the Japanese embassy.
Political analysts say the key election is next March when President Suharto, 75, is widely expected to run for a seventh five-year term.
There is keen interest in who he will approve as a running mate, who could be a potential successor.
